opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most important shifts happening in AI right now, and honestly it's still a bit underappreciated.

For a long time, especially in computer vision, the dominant paradigm was supervised learning: you have an image, a human attaches a label like "cat" or "dog," and the model learns to map pixels to that label. Even with the move toward vision-language models, the supervision signal is still essentially human language. The model learns about the visual world through the lens of the words we chose to describe it. That's powerful, but it's also a bottleneck. Language is a very compressed, lossy description of reality. When I say "a cup falls off a table," I'm leaving out almost everything that actually matters physically: the trajectory, how the liquid splashes, the light, the sound, the way it shatters.

What video generation, and generative modeling of raw data more broadly, does is flip the objective. Instead of asking the model to predict a label or a caption, you ask it to model the distribution of the data itself, every pixel across time. To generate a plausible video of that cup falling, the model has to implicitly capture something about gravity, object permanence, materials, lighting, and causality. Nobody wrote those rules down. They have to emerge from the data.

So I see it as moving from learning *what humans say about the world* to learning *the world itself*. Language models succeeded partly because text is both the input and the supervision. Next-token prediction on text is self-supervised, so it scales with data rather than with annotation effort. Video offers an analogous opportunity for the physical world, and the amount of visual data dwarfs text.

That said, I want to be careful about overclaiming. Generating pixels that look right isn't the same as having a good internal model of the world. A lot of current video models are excellent at texture and appearance and still make basic physical mistakes. Objects merge, hands deform, things appear and disappear. There's also an open question about whether pixel-level reconstruction is even the right objective, or whether you're spending enormous capacity on details that don't matter for understanding. That's partly why I'm interested in approaches that learn good representations, not just good samples. The ideal is a model where generation and understanding reinforce each other, rather than generation being a pretty rendering engine sitting on top.

So my short answer is that modeling data directly removes the human-language bottleneck and gives us a path to scale toward something like a world model. But generation is a means, not the end. The real goal is a system that genuinely understands how the visual and physical world works, and we're still early on that path.

r003.rationale: It contrasts labels with modeling pixels across time and says this requires capturing information such as gravity, materials, lighting, and causality that labels omit.

r004.rationale: It describes moving away from language-based supervision, but does not interpret that shift as a bitter-lesson move.

r005.rationale: It questions whether pixel-level reconstruction is the right objective and favors useful representations, but does not frame this as pixels being insufficiently bitter-lesson-oriented.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the cleanest way to put it is that we spent a decade teaching models to describe the world, and now we're asking them to actually simulate it.

In the supervised era, the signal was a label. A human looked at an image and said "cat," and the model's whole job was to compress the pixels down to that one token of information. Language models are a richer version of the same idea. Text is an extremely dense, human-curated description of the world, so predicting the next word gets you a lot of knowledge for free. But it's still a description. It's a shadow of reality that someone already decided was worth writing down.

Video is different. Nobody labeled the physics in a video. The way light falls across a surface, the way a cup tips before it spills, the way a person's weight shifts before they take a step, none of that is annotated. It's just there in the pixels, and it's there in enormous quantity. So when you train a model to generate video, you're forcing it to model the data-generating process itself. If it wants to produce a plausible next frame, it has to internalize something about object permanence, about occlusion, about causality in time. The supervision comes from the structure of the world rather than from a human writing captions.

That's why I think of it as moving from modeling "what someone said about the world" to modeling "the world." And honestly, that's the original promise of self-supervised learning. We talked about it for years in vision, and I think video generation is where it finally gets serious, because the prediction task is hard enough that shortcuts don't work.

I'll add one caveat, because I think people overstate this too. Generating convincing video does not automatically mean the model understands physics in a way that transfers. You can get very far on surface statistics. The open question, and this is what I spend a lot of my time on, is whether the representations inside these generative models are actually good for understanding, or whether generation and understanding are pulling in different directions. My intuition is that they should converge, but we haven't proven it yet. Right now the representations learned purely from generation are often worse for recognition tasks than the ones from discriminative pretraining, and figuring out why is, to me, one of the most interesting problems in the field.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generating video from pixels, but does not identify data x as the target in P(x|y) or y as conditioning information.

r002.rationale: It describes a classifier reducing an image to a label, but does not say its likelihood assignments compete among the available labels.

r003.rationale: It says video generation must capture unlabelled world structure such as object permanence, occlusion, and causality, whereas label modeling compresses an image to a single token.

r004.rationale: The response contrasts pixel-based video modeling with human-curated language descriptions, but does not frame this as a bitter-lesson move away from language-supplied structure.

r005.rationale: Its caveat concerns whether generated video implies transferable understanding; it does not suggest that pixels are an insufficiently bitter-lesson-oriented representation.

astra-6.text:
我觉得这个转变的核心，是我们开始从数据本身获得学习信号，而不只是学习人给数据赋予的标签。以前做视频理解，我们可能给一段视频标注“一个人在跑步”，然后训练模型预测这个标签。但这几个字其实丢掉了大量信息：这个人怎么迈步，身体怎么保持平衡，镜头怎么移动，光影怎么变化。

当你去做视频生成时，这些细节就变成了模型必须面对的问题。你不能只知道“跑步”这个概念，还需要生成一个在时间上连续、在视觉上合理的过程。从这个意义上说，建模的目标从一个高度压缩的语义描述，转向了数据里更丰富的结构。

当然，这不意味着语言不重要。语言仍然是很好的交互和控制方式，但它不必是学习信号的全部。真正有意思的问题是：为了生成这些数据，模型究竟学到了多少关于世界的规律？它可能学到运动、空间关系和某些物理上的约束，但生成得像，并不自动等于理解了因果。这是我觉得需要区分、也值得继续研究的地方。

r003.rationale: It says labels omit detail and data contains richer structure, but only asks how much the model learns about world rules and says it may learn some. It does not clearly claim that modeling the data distribution requires substantially more world knowledge than modeling labels.

r004.rationale: The response discusses data versus semantic descriptions and says language remains useful, but does not frame direct pixel modeling as a bitter-lesson move away from language-supplied structure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key shift is in what we ask the model to learn. In a recognition task, you take a very rich signal—a video—and compress it into a label or a sentence. That’s useful, but the supervision only captures a small part of what’s happening. A label like “someone picks up a cup” doesn’t describe the motion of the fingers, the lighting, or how the cup interacts with the table.

When you model the video itself, those details become part of the learning problem. The model has to capture enough of the structure of the data to generate it. Language can still provide an interface or a condition, but it’s no longer the entire target.

That makes video generation interesting as a route toward learning about the world. But I would distinguish generating convincing videos from understanding the underlying dynamics. A model can learn patterns that look right without having a reliable grasp of causality. The question is how far this richer learning signal can take us, and how we measure what the model has actually learned.

r001.rationale: The response says the model learns the video itself and that language can condition it, but does not identify a probability target P(x|y) with data x as the target and y as conditioning information.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss classifiers or how their likelihood assignments compete among a fixed set of labels.

r003.rationale: It notes that labels omit video details, but does not claim that modeling the data distribution requires substantially more information about the world than modeling labels.

r004.rationale: It says language need not be the entire target, but does not interpret direct pixel modeling as a bitter-lesson move away from language-supplied structure.

r005.rationale: The caveat concerns whether convincing video generation demonstrates understanding of dynamics; it does not suggest that pixels remain an insufficiently bitter-lesson-oriented representation.
